memorableLines.why: It turns the chapter into an actionable rule.

chapters.title: The Mechanics of Pre-suasion: Causes, Constraints, and Correctives
chapters.hook: The first screen on the triage tablet can ready shame before symptoms are even sorted.
chapters.counterintuition: Prepared concepts are not commands. They are temporary activations that help or distort depending on relevance, limits, and the corrective you place nearby.
chapters.tryThisNow: Find one first cue in a form or script. Write what it readies, what it could distort, and the correction that should appear before the decision.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Pre-suasion works by readying concepts, so check the cause and the boundary before trusting any opening cue.

breakdown.fastRead:
A triage tablet pauses on insurance before symptoms. Patients answer pain questions differently after thinking about coverage. The nurse manager moves the insurance screen later and compares the responses. The prepared concept changed the next answer.

This is the mechanics level. A cue readies a concept, and a readied concept is easier to activate when the next information arrives. The cue still has limits. If it distorts the wrong answer, the sequence needs a corrective.
breakdown.deepRead:
A court administrator reorders a jury questionnaire. Neighborhood questions once appeared before evidence instructions, and later fairness ratings shifted around assumptions the form never meant to raise. She moves those questions after the instruction sheet and tracks what changes.

Readied is not the same as controlled.

The source support makes a careful claim: pre-suasion focuses recipients first on concepts associatively aligned with information still to come. Mental elements fire not only when ready, but when readied. That explains the effect without turning it into mystery or permanent programming.

A loan script shows the constraint. If the opening recites balance due, callers may hear hardship options through shame. A neutral identity check before the option sheet can reduce that spillover. The corrective is not cosmetic. It changes which concept is active when help is offered.

There is a small habit that catches most mechanics errors. Read the first item, the second item, and the last item out loud, then ask what concept sits in the room after each one. If the concept matches the decision the form is supposed to support, the order is honest. If it points sideways, the order is doing work nobody asked it to do.
breakdown.fullRead:
A glowing answer button under a science-museum question panel can ready curiosity. That is useful if the next label honors uncertainty. It is misleading if the exhibit makes a guess feel like a fact. The designer adds a correction label beside the mystery prompt before visitors press the answer button: what we know, what we are still testing.

Mechanics keep the practice honest. A cue has a cause: it makes some concept easier to activate. A cue has constraints: the effect is temporary, context-bound, and vulnerable to mismatch. A cue needs correctives when it might spread beyond the decision it should inform.

Look at the restaurant menu owner testing health icons. A red icon beside a balanced dish may ready caution so strongly that diners avoid the dish for the wrong reason. The sales tally does not prove the icon is bad. It asks whether the cue’s reach exceeded its job.

A university advising office tried the same audit. The intake question "what is going wrong this semester" had been first on the form for years. Counselors moved it after a quieter question about one thing students wanted to keep doing. Stress reports still appeared. Plans built around them now mentioned protective routines twice as often. The form had not removed the problem. It had readied a different concept beside the problem.

What did the first cue make easier to think, and where should that ease stop?

An HR analyst sees the word complaint at the top of a feedback survey and worries it will ready resentment across every answer. She removes it from the opener and adds a later corrective item that asks for one working practice to preserve. The survey still collects problems. It no longer primes the whole form as grievance.

An education researcher names the same effect for teachers. A test that opens with a definition question primes recall. A test that opens with a scenario question primes application. The same students, the same chapter, the same hour. The first item is not just the first item. It is a cue that decides what mental engine warms up before the rest of the test arrives.

A clinic adopting a new screening tool added a small two-line correction beneath the first question. The correction read: these items measure today, not tomorrow. Patients who feared bad numbers reported less catastrophizing in the follow-up note. The cue did not stop the test. It stopped the test from spreading. A correction is cheap when the wrong reading would have cost a real visit.

Mechanics also asks who built the cue. A team copying a template from another industry will get the wave of a concept without the calibration. Borrowed tests carry borrowed primes. Before adopting a form, read the first three items and ask whether you would willingly answer them in this domain on a hard day.

The clean use of mechanics is humble. You do not plant any idea and make it work. You ready one relevant concept, watch for spillover, and build a correction where fairness requires it.

examples.title: Erin Moves Insurance After Symptoms

planSpec.audience: a nurse manager checking whether a pain-scale prompt readies the wrong concern
planSpec.stakes: whether a prepared concept helps or distorts the next answer
planSpec.requiredBeat: the manager compares responses when insurance questions come before versus after symptom sorting

examples.scenario: A triage tablet pauses on the insurance screen while Erin lays a symptom card beside it. In the postmortem, she compares pain-scale responses from days when coverage questions came first with days when symptoms came first. The answers shift. Erin is not inventing a protocol; she is deciding whether the first screen readied money worries before patients described pain.
examples.whatToDo: Move insurance questions after symptom sorting and compare response patterns. Keep the coverage screen from readying the wrong concern.
examples.whyItMatters: A first concept can color the next answer. The sequence matters when money anxiety may distort clinical description.

examples.title: Victoria Reorders the Neighborhood Tabs

planSpec.audience: a court administrator testing whether early questions bias later fairness ratings
planSpec.stakes: whether readied concepts can be corrected by order changes
planSpec.requiredBeat: the administrator moves neighborhood questions after evidence instructions and tracks what changes

examples.scenario: A questionnaire packet with reordered tabs sits beside an instruction sheet as Victoria reviews juror forms. At 1:10 p.m. in the courthouse form room, Victoria is the court administrator deciding which question order will be tested before summons packets print. Neighborhood questions used to appear before fairness ratings. She must decide before printing whether to keep the old order or move those tabs after the evidence instructions and track changes. The new order tests whether a readied place concept was leaking into judgments it should not touch.
examples.whatToDo: Move neighborhood questions after evidence instructions and compare fairness ratings. Use order as a corrective, not as a hidden lever.
examples.whyItMatters: The place concept may be relevant later, but early activation can spill into fairness ratings before evidence rules are clear.

examples.title: Monica Strikes the Balance Line First

planSpec.audience: a bank compliance officer limiting priming by debt language
planSpec.stakes: whether callers are readied for shame before hearing options
planSpec.requiredBeat: the officer replaces the opening balance recitation with a neutral identity check and compares take-up

examples.scenario: A call script lies on Monica’s desk with the balance line struck through and a hardship option sheet underneath. Before the edit, callers heard the amount due first and often declined help. After the edit, the opening is a neutral identity check, then options. Monica compares take-up and listens for shame in the call notes. She is deciding whether the old first sentence readied the wrong self.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the opening balance recitation with a neutral identity check, then present hardship options clearly.
examples.whyItMatters: Debt language can ready shame before help appears. The correction lets callers hear options before the balance defines the conversation.

examples.title: Jonas Adds the Uncertainty Label

planSpec.audience: an exhibit designer showing uncertainty without making guesses feel like facts
planSpec.stakes: whether readied curiosity stays inside evidence limits
planSpec.requiredBeat: the designer adds a correction label beside the mystery prompt before visitors press the answer button

examples.scenario: An exhibit button glows under a question panel while Jonas holds a correction label. At 2:45 p.m. on the museum floor, Jonas is the exhibit lead deciding how to keep the correction visible before visitors press the answer button. Visitors are about to decide whether the mystery answer is settled fact. Before the answer button opens, he adds a label that says what is known and what remains under test. Curiosity still pulls them in, but the correction sits beside the cue before the guess hardens.
examples.whatToDo: Place the correction label beside the mystery prompt before visitors press the answer button. Let curiosity meet its evidence limits immediately.
examples.whyItMatters: Mystery readies belief in an answer. The correction keeps curiosity from turning a provisional explanation into certainty.

examples.title: Greta Tests the Red Icon’s Reach

planSpec.audience: a menu owner testing if health icons crowd out taste decisions too strongly
planSpec.stakes: whether a cue’s reach exceeds the decision it should inform
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner checks whether diners avoid balanced dishes with one red icon before changing the icon system

examples.scenario: A menu proof shows red icons beside three entrees while Greta compares the sales tally. At 11:30 a.m. in the cafe office, Greta is the menu owner deciding whether the red icon makes diners think health or danger. In the postmortem, one balanced dish with a single red icon fell harder than richer dishes without icons. She checks whether diners avoided it as unhealthy before changing the system. The cue was meant to inform, not make one mark define the whole plate.
examples.whatToDo: Compare sales by icon pattern before redesigning the menu. Keep health cues from reaching beyond the specific information they carry.
examples.whyItMatters: A red icon can ready caution so strongly that taste and balance disappear. The tally tests whether the cue exceeded its useful limit.

examples.title: Henrik Removes Complaint From the Opener

planSpec.audience: an HR analyst preventing one word from contaminating all answers
planSpec.stakes: whether readied resentment spreads beyond the target issue
planSpec.requiredBeat: the analyst removes the word complaint from the opener and adds a later corrective item

examples.scenario: A survey preview shows the first prompt highlighted while Henrik studies a response heatmap from last quarter. The word complaint sat in the opener and seemed to pull resentment through unrelated answers. He removes it and adds a later corrective item asking what should be preserved. The survey still invites problems, but the first concept no longer contaminates the whole form.
examples.whatToDo: Remove complaint from the opener and add a later preserve item. Let criticism appear where it belongs without readying resentment everywhere.
examples.whyItMatters: One early word can activate a frame across the survey. The corrective restores range so every answer is not pulled toward grievance.

questions.prompt: A triage form asks insurance questions before symptom sorting, and pain answers change. What is the likely mechanism? At triage intake, the nurse manager must decide whether the first screen readies money worries before symptom answers.
choices: Insurance questions are always irrelevant in emergency rooms.
Coverage concerns may be readied before patients describe symptoms.
Pain answers are too subjective to use.
questions.explanation: The order may activate money anxiety before pain reporting. The point is not that coverage never matters, but that early activation can distort the next answer.

questions.prompt: A jury questionnaire asks neighborhood questions before fairness ratings. What corrective best tests spillover? Before the jury form is printed, the administrator must decide how to test whether neighborhood questions are spilling into fairness ratings.
choices: Delete every neighborhood question.
Move those questions after evidence instructions and track rating changes.
Tell jurors not to be biased.
questions.explanation: Reordering tests whether the early concept was contaminating fairness ratings. Deletion may lose useful information, and a warning alone may not change activation.

questions.prompt: A hardship call opens with the balance due, and callers decline options. What should the compliance officer try? During a compliance review of the call script, the officer must decide whether balance-first wording readies shame before help appears.
choices: Repeat the balance more slowly so callers understand it.
Hide the balance until after enrollment.
Open with a neutral identity check, then present the option sheet.
questions.explanation: A neutral opener reduces shame activation before help appears. Repeating the balance may deepen the problem, while hiding it removes relevant information.

questions.prompt: A museum mystery prompt makes visitors treat a guess as settled fact. Which correction fits? On the museum floor, the exhibit lead must decide how to keep curiosity open without letting the first guess become false certainty.
choices: Remove all curiosity from the exhibit.
Make the answer button larger.
Add a label beside the prompt showing what is known and what remains under test.
questions.explanation: The correction keeps curiosity inside evidence limits. Removing curiosity wastes a useful magnetizer, and a larger button would intensify the same problem.

questions.prompt: A red nutrition icon makes diners avoid a balanced dish. What should the menu owner ask? Before the menu goes to print, the owner must decide whether the red icon readies health or warning in the wrong place.
choices: Whether diners are too emotional to read menus.
Whether the icon’s caution cue exceeded the exact information it should carry.
Whether all nutrition information should be hidden.
questions.explanation: The issue is cue reach. The icon may ready caution beyond its intended scope; insulting diners or hiding all information misses the corrective test.

questions.prompt: A survey opener uses the word complaint, and unrelated answers become harsher. What revision is strongest? In a survey preview, the analyst must decide whether the first word readies complaint mode before unrelated questions begin.
choices: Add a cheerful image above the complaint prompt.
Keep the opener and tell employees to be balanced.
Use a neutral opener and add a later item asking what should be preserved.
questions.explanation: The neutral opener prevents broad resentment activation, and the preserve item corrects range. Cheerful images and instructions do not address the readied concept.

questions.prompt: Someone says priming can plant any idea and make people act. What is the best reply?
choices: Readied concepts can influence what comes next, but relevance, timing, and correctives limit the effect.
Priming is fake because people always decide consciously.
Priming works forever once the cue appears.
questions.explanation: The answer keeps the mechanism and the limits together. The other choices deny the effect or exaggerate it into permanent control.

questions.prompt: A form opens with “fraud warning” before asking users to rate ordinary service quality. Ratings fall sharply. What should be evaluated?
choices: Whether users dislike warnings in general.
Whether fraud language readied suspicion that spilled into unrelated ratings.
Whether all service ratings are unreliable.
questions.explanation: The early warning may activate suspicion beyond its proper target. The corrective is to test placement and scope, not dismiss ratings altogether.

questions.prompt: A designer wants to use a curiosity cue before a medical-risk explanation. Which plan is most responsible?
choices: Open a question the explanation answers, and place uncertainty limits next to the cue.
Open with the most frightening mystery possible.
Withhold the answer until users agree to the recommendation.
questions.explanation: The responsible plan pairs activation with an immediate corrective. Fear and withholding both exploit the opened loop rather than helping people judge.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean for a concept to be readied?
reviewCards.back: A cue has made the concept easier to activate when the next information arrives. It is influence, not control.

reviewCards.front: A form asks money questions before pain questions. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: The early cue may ready money anxiety and distort symptom reporting. Move it later and compare responses.

reviewCards.front: What are the three checks on a prepared concept?
reviewCards.back: Cause, constraint, and corrective: what it readies, where the effect should stop, and what prevents spillover.

reviewCards.front: Why add an uncertainty label beside a mystery prompt?
reviewCards.back: Curiosity readies belief in an answer. The label keeps visitors inside the evidence rather than letting mystery harden into certainty.

reviewCards.front: A survey starts with complaint and everything sounds harsher. What is the fix?
reviewCards.back: Use a neutral opener and add a later corrective item that asks what should be preserved, so criticism does not swallow the whole form.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is auditing the first cue for activation and spillover. You ask what concept the cue readies, whether that concept belongs, and what correction keeps judgment fair.

ifThenPlans.plan: If an early form question may ready shame or suspicion, then move it after neutral sorting and compare responses.
If a call opens with debt language, then test a neutral identity check before presenting help.
If curiosity is used, then place the evidence limit beside the question before the answer appears.
If one word may contaminate every answer, then replace it in the opener and add a later balancing item.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find the first cue in one form, script, or meeting. Write three lines: readies, distorts, corrects. Change the cue if the corrective is missing.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit a sequence of questions or screens. Move one cue later, add one corrective, and record whether the answers become cleaner.

memorableLines.text: Readied is not the same as controlled.
memorableLines.why: It keeps the mechanism bounded and credible.

memorableLines.text: Mechanics keep the practice honest.
memorableLines.why: It frames the chapter as disciplined testing rather than mystique.

memorableLines.text: You ready one relevant concept, watch for spillover, and build a correction where fairness requires it.
memorableLines.why: It summarizes cause, constraint, and corrective in one actionable line.

chapters.title: Six Main Roads to Change: Broad Boulevards as Smart Shortcuts
chapters.hook: Twelve circled winter beds make scarcity cleaner than any deadline banner.
chapters.counterintuition: The six principles are not buttons to press in sequence. The smart move is to frontload the one principle that honestly fits the choice and leave the others alone.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one request and circle one fitting principle: reciprocity, liking, authority, social proof, scarcity, or consistency. Delete cues for the rest.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Frontload the single influence shortcut that truthfully belongs to the decision, rather than mixing principles until someone complies.

breakdown.fastRead:
A farm-share manager opens a laminated field map. Only twelve winter beds are circled. The renewal envelope comes after the map, not before. Scarcity is real here because the beds are real. A countdown banner would only cheapen the request.

The classic roads are giving first, warmth, earned expertise, visible peers, real limits, and prior commitments. Each can guide attention before an ask. Choose the road that fits; do not pile all six into one setup.
breakdown.deepRead:
A tool-library coordinator gives residents a blade-sharpening voucher before showing the annual membership card. Reciprocity fits because useful help comes first and the ask follows in the open. It would not fit if the voucher hid a fee.

One road is enough. Stacking principles makes a setup feel engineered, not optimized.

The six classic principles are reciprocity, liking, authority, social proof, scarcity, and consistency. They can steer choices, so a setup can make the right one stand out before the request. Right is the key word. The fit between principle and decision is what makes the shortcut honest, not the cleverness of the setup.

A medical conference organizer can make authority visible when a speaker's trial role bears on the protocol. A choir director can use consistency when singers have already named the show they promised not to miss. When every principle appears at once, the setup starts to feel rigged.

The hardest discipline is leaving five of the six on the floor when only one fits. The other principles are still true. They simply do not belong to this choice on this day. Treat them as honest tools you are not using right now. The audience will then hear the one tool you did use as a fair signal rather than a stack.
breakdown.fullRead:
The field map with twelve circled beds does a narrow job. It tells CSA members that winter capacity is limited. It does not pretend the deadline is earlier than it is. It does not claim neighbors are signing up if they are not. It lets scarcity be the relevant shortcut because physical beds are the constraint.

The same discipline applies to the other roads. Social proof belongs when a solar co-op organizer can show an actual map of signed-up roofs. Liking belongs when a craft-fair curator notices a maker’s material choice from the application before explaining booth limits. Authority belongs when expertise directly bears on the recommendation. Reciprocity belongs when a useful first gift is real. Consistency belongs when people have already made a standard their own.

A volunteer recruiter at a community garden once tried all six in one Saturday afternoon. She handed out free seed packets and reminded people of a long-standing neighborhood promise. She mentioned how many beds were filled, named a master gardener on the panel, said only three slots remained, and complimented a sun hat. The plot sat empty the next week. Each shortcut was true in isolation. Together they made the offer feel like a sales pitch. When the recruiter came back in the spring and used only the bed map with the names of last year's gardeners pencilled in, half the morning's visitors signed up.

Which road would still make sense if the audience asked to see the evidence?

The danger is principle stacking. A request that opens with a free gift, a credential, a deadline, a popularity count, a personal compliment, and a prior commitment does not feel optimized. It feels trapped. Each shortcut weakens when it is thrown in without fit.

There is also a discipline of removal. A real-estate office used to print "priced to sell", a five-star testimonial, an agent badge, and a countdown timer on every flyer. The office removed every cue except the testimonial, and only when it actually came from the buyer of the previous home. Calls went up. The flyer stopped looking like signage. It started looking like a recommendation from a neighbor.

Choose the principle that tells the cleanest truth about the decision. Then make that principle visible before the ask. A map, a voucher, a badge slide, a calendar mark, a roof sticker, a sample swatch: each object should point to one road.

The setup is small once you have committed to one principle. A page, a map, an object, a sentence in the right order. The work shifts from designing a multi-lever apparatus to telling a single true thing first. People notice the difference even when they cannot articulate it. Their slowness stops feeling like resistance because the message has stopped feeling like a system. Often the room relaxes a beat before the ask, and that beat is what the setup was paying for.

A shortcut is smart only when it shortens the right path.

examples.title: Anna Hands Over the Sharpening Voucher

planSpec.audience: a coordinator choosing reciprocity before a membership ask
planSpec.stakes: whether a small useful loan should come before the fee request
planSpec.requiredBeat: the coordinator hands residents a free blade-sharpening voucher before showing the annual membership card

examples.scenario: A sharpening voucher lies beside a row of loaner drills while Anna greets residents at the tool-library launch. The annual membership card is still under the table. She is about to decide whether to lead with the fee or give a useful blade-sharpening voucher first. The voucher is real, limited to one service, and tied to the tools residents came to borrow.
examples.whatToDo: Give the useful sharpening voucher before showing the membership card. Let reciprocity arise from actual value, not from a trinket.
examples.whyItMatters: Reciprocity fits because residents receive help connected to the library’s purpose before they are asked to join.

examples.title: Drake Highlights the Trial Role

planSpec.audience: an organizer choosing authority before a clinical guideline session
planSpec.stakes: whether credentials must be salient before the recommendation
planSpec.requiredBeat: the organizer places the speaker’s trial role on the badge slide before the protocol ask appears

examples.scenario: A badge slide shows one credential line highlighted while Drake places a protocol card on each chair. Attendees must decide whether to trust a new clinical guideline session. Before the protocol ask appears, the speaker’s role in the relevant trial is visible on the screen. The authority cue is not a prestige parade; it names why this person can speak to this recommendation.
examples.whatToDo: Highlight the trial role on the badge slide before showing the protocol card. Use authority only where expertise directly supports the ask.
examples.whyItMatters: Authority works when the credential answers the audience’s evidence question. Unrelated status would only decorate the recommendation.

examples.title: Sigrid Shows the Twelve Winter Beds

planSpec.audience: a CSA manager choosing scarcity before late-season renewals
planSpec.stakes: whether limited beds are real and should be named before signup
planSpec.requiredBeat: the manager shows the actual field map with only twelve winter beds left before opening renewals

examples.scenario: A laminated field map has twelve winter beds circled while Sigrid stacks renewal envelopes beside it. At 6:00 p.m. in the farm-share pickup barn, Sigrid is the manager deciding how to show the winter-bed limit before renewals are signed. Members are about to decide whether to renew late-season shares. She must choose whether to send a deadline email or show the actual bed map before opening renewals. The scarcity is visible, countable, and tied to soil, not to a made-up timer.
examples.whatToDo: Show the field map with twelve beds before handing out renewal envelopes. Let real capacity define scarcity.
examples.whyItMatters: Scarcity is clean when the limit exists outside the message. A false deadline would create pressure without truth.

examples.title: Peter Marks the Performance Promise

planSpec.audience: a director choosing consistency before asking for rehearsals
planSpec.stakes: whether members should recall their own standard before committing
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director asks singers to mark the performance they promised not to miss before handing out the rehearsal calendar

examples.scenario: A rehearsal calendar sits under a pencil-written performance date while Peter watches singers gather their folders. He asks them to mark the performance they promised not to miss before he hands out the attendance pledge. The room does not feel scolded. It feels reminded. The rehearsal commitment now connects to a standard the singers had already named for themselves.
examples.whatToDo: Ask singers to mark the promised performance before the rehearsal calendar appears. Let consistency point to their own standard.
examples.whyItMatters: Consistency works without guilt when people see the commitment they already made, then choose the rehearsal behavior that supports it.

examples.title: Isabel Places Roof Stickers Beside the Form

planSpec.audience: an organizer choosing social proof before home assessments
planSpec.stakes: whether visible neighbor participation lowers uncertainty
planSpec.requiredBeat: the organizer places a map of signed-up roofs beside the assessment form before mentioning rebates

examples.scenario: A neighborhood map dotted with roof stickers sits beside Isabel’s assessment form. At 9:20 a.m. on a neighborhood assessment route, Isabel is the organizer deciding whether roof stickers are useful proof or pressure. Before the map, homeowners asked whether they would be the only house trying solar. After the map, they ask which installer slots remain. Isabel still mentions rebates, but only after real neighbor participation has lowered uncertainty. Her decision is whether to let social proof speak before incentives.
examples.whatToDo: Place the signed-up roof map beside the assessment form before discussing rebates. Let actual neighbor participation reduce uncertainty.
examples.whyItMatters: Social proof fits when the map is true. The stickers show people like them already taking the same step.

examples.title: Mathieu Starts With the Linen Swatch

planSpec.audience: a curator choosing liking before compliance with booth rules
planSpec.stakes: whether shared taste should be visible before a hard constraint
planSpec.requiredBeat: the curator comments on one maker’s material choice from the application before explaining the strict booth footprint

examples.scenario: A sample swatch lies beside a booth-layout card as Mathieu meets a ceramics maker. At 4:00 p.m. beside the trade-show booth plan, Mathieu is the sales lead deciding whether the swatch should support liking or distract from fit. “The linen backing in your application made the glaze read softer,” he says. Then he turns to the strict booth footprint. The maker must decide whether the rule is a cold constraint or a constraint explained by someone who has actually seen the work. Mathieu chooses shared taste before compliance.
examples.whatToDo: Comment specifically on the material choice from the application, then explain the booth footprint. Keep liking grounded in observed taste.
examples.whyItMatters: Liking fits when it comes from genuine attention to the maker’s work. Flattery would make the hard rule feel slippery.

questions.prompt: A tool library gives residents a real sharpening voucher before showing membership cards. Which principle is being frontloaded?
choices: Reciprocity, because useful value comes before the ask.
Scarcity, because tools are limited.
Authority, because the coordinator runs the event.
questions.explanation: The voucher creates a genuine give-before-ask sequence, so reciprocity fits. Tool limits and coordinator role may exist, but they are not the main cue.

questions.prompt: A medical organizer highlights a speaker’s role in the exact clinical trial before a protocol recommendation. Why is this a clean authority cue?
choices: It makes the speaker seem impressive in general.
The credential directly bears on the recommendation being made.
It prevents attendees from asking hard questions.
questions.explanation: Authority fits because the trial role answers why this speaker should discuss the protocol. General impressiveness or silencing questions would misuse the shortcut.

questions.prompt: A CSA manager shows a field map with twelve winter beds left before renewals. What separates this from false urgency? At the winter share renewal table, the manager must decide whether the field map shows a real limit or manufactures pressure.
choices: The map is laminated and looks official.
The limit is visible, countable, and outside the message.
The deadline email uses stronger wording.
questions.explanation: Real scarcity rests on an actual constraint. Lamination and stronger wording only change presentation, not whether the shortage is true.

questions.prompt: A choir director asks singers to mark the performance they promised not to miss before handing out rehearsal calendars. Which shortcut fits?
choices: Social proof, because many singers are present.
Liking, because the director is warm.
Consistency, because the new commitment connects to their own prior standard.
questions.explanation: The marked performance activates consistency with a standard singers already chose. The room’s size and the director’s warmth are not the active principle.

questions.prompt: A solar organizer places a map of signed-up roofs beside assessment forms. When is this ethical social proof? On a porch-assessment route, the organizer must decide when visible neighbor signups are evidence and when they become pressure.
choices: When the map makes the neighborhood look fuller than it is.
When rebates are hidden until after signatures.
When the roof stickers reflect actual participating neighbors.
questions.explanation: Social proof is clean when participation is real. Inflated maps or hidden rebate details pressure decisions by distorting evidence.

questions.prompt: A craft curator compliments a maker’s material choice before explaining a strict booth footprint. What keeps liking from becoming flattery?
choices: The comment is specific to the application and connects to real shared taste.
The curator smiles while delivering the rule.
The maker receives a bigger booth afterward.
questions.explanation: Specific observed taste makes liking credible. A smile can be empty, and changing the rule is not what makes the principle honest.

questions.prompt: A fundraiser opens with a gift, a celebrity quote, a countdown, a popularity claim, and a personal compliment. What is the likely problem?
choices: The ask may feel engineered because too many shortcuts are stacked without fit.
The fundraiser forgot to include scarcity.
The audience needs all six principles every time.
questions.explanation: Principle stacking feels like pressure when the cues do not all belong. The skill is choosing the one honest route, not loading the request with every possible lever.

questions.prompt: A clinic wants patients to follow a new check-in rule. Which cue should come first if the real reason is expert safety review?
choices: A note that every other patient likes the rule.
The safety nurse’s relevant review role beside the check-in card.
A claim that slots are almost gone.
questions.explanation: Authority fits if expert review is the true reason. Popularity and scarcity would be mismatched shortcuts if they do not explain the rule.

questions.prompt: Before framing a request, what is the best first question about the six principles? Before choosing any opening cue, the planner must decide which influence road truthfully belongs to this request.
choices: Which principle can get compliance fastest?
How many principles can be combined without seeming obvious?
Which single principle truthfully fits this choice?
questions.explanation: The right first question is fit. Speed and stealth turn the principles into tricks, while a truthful match keeps the setup defensible.

reviewCards.front: You are choosing the one influence shortcut for your next ask. Which six broad roads make up the candidate list?
reviewCards.back: Reciprocity, liking, authority, social proof, scarcity, and consistency. Pick the single principle that truthfully fits the choice, then frontload it.

reviewCards.front: A field map shows twelve real beds left. Which principle is active?
reviewCards.back: Scarcity. The limit is physical and visible, so naming it before renewal helps people judge capacity honestly.

reviewCards.front: What makes consistency clean in a rehearsal pledge?
reviewCards.back: Singers recall a performance they already promised not to miss, then choose rehearsal behavior that matches their own standard.

reviewCards.front: Why is principle stacking risky?
reviewCards.back: Multiple cues without fit make the request feel engineered. One honest shortcut is stronger than six mismatched ones.

reviewCards.front: How do you choose the right broad road?
reviewCards.back: Ask which principle truthfully explains the decision and what evidence you can show before the request.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is selecting one influence principle that truly fits. You then make that principle visible before the request with a concrete cue that can withstand explanation.

ifThenPlans.plan: If reciprocity fits, then provide real useful value before showing the membership ask.
If authority fits, then show the relevant credential before the protocol or rule appears.
If scarcity fits, then show the actual constraint before any deadline language.
If social proof fits, then show real participation before discussing incentives.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one upcoming request and write the six principle names. Cross out five. For the remaining one, write the evidence that makes it honest.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, audit one persuasive setup for principle stacking. Remove any cue that does not truthfully belong to the decision.

memorableLines.text: Stacking principles makes a setup feel engineered, not optimized.
memorableLines.why: It names the failure mode of principle stacking in a quotable line.

memorableLines.text: A shortcut is smart only when it shortens the right path.
memorableLines.why: It distinguishes ethical fit from manipulation.

memorableLines.text: The fit between principle and decision is what makes the shortcut honest, not the cleverness of the setup.
memorableLines.why: It states fit as the working standard for choosing one principle over another.

chapters.title: Unity 1: Being Together
chapters.hook: The old postmark matters before the fragile letters ever leave the family table.
chapters.counterintuition: Unity is not friendliness. It is a We relationship made conscious through legitimate identity, family, or place before cooperation is requested.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before asking for help, write the real We that already exists. If the phrase sounds borrowed, flattering, or vague, do not use it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Unity works when a legitimate shared identity is brought forward before the request, making cooperation feel like care for one of us.

breakdown.fastRead:
An archivist sets a yellowed envelope on the table and names the street both families left behind. Only then does she open the loan agreement for the fragile letters. The trust request now sits inside a shared origin, not across a counter.

Unity is deeper than liking. It is a real We, built from shared identity. Family and place cues can bring that bond forward before a request. The cue has to be earned. Fake closeness breaks the trust unity is meant to create.
breakdown.deepRead:
A county birth registry lies open under a clinic lamp. Three nursing applicants see their family names on the page before the shift roster appears. The doctor is not saying the job is easy. She is making place identity visible before asking people to serve the county that raised them.

We is a serious word. It names a bond that already exists, not one being negotiated in the moment.

Source support identifies unity as an additional principle of influence, distinct from the familiar six. A shared identity can increase acceptance, cooperation, liking, help, trust, and assent when it is brought forward before the ask. The first route uses cues tied to family and place.

That boundary matters. A shared hometown, family mark, campus doorway, clan greeting, or arrival map can create togetherness when it is real. A fake We can sound warm and still be theft.

The cleanest test is asking whether the person inside the We would name it themselves without prompting. If they would, the unity cue is part of their world. If they would not, the cue is being lent only while the request is on the table, and it will be returned with interest. The cost of borrowing identity is small the first time and large the third.
breakdown.fullRead:
A repaired net lies across a dock crate while siblings argue about buying a new boat engine. The budget sheet is ready, but the adviser first asks each sibling to name the net-mending mark their grandfather taught them. The mark is small. The shared identity is not.

This is unity by being together. The request is not, like me. It is, remember what we are part of. That difference separates unity from ordinary rapport. Rapport can make a person pleasant to hear. Unity can make a request feel like care for a shared body.

A neighborhood council learned this with a flood-grant meeting. The chair started by reading the names of the original ten families who built houses on the block in 1972. Some of those names still lived there. Some had moved a generation ago. By the time the grant application was on the table, the meeting had already remembered itself as a group with a history. It was not a list of address numbers waiting for money.

A developer asking elders to record pronunciations for a language app can play a child saying the clan greeting before showing the consent form. The greeting belongs to the group before it belongs to the app. A college officer can show the flooded doorway every graduate used as a first-year student before opening the gift field for repairs. The doorway says, this place held us.

A tribal health center uses the move with a clean conscience because the cue is the truth of the place. New nurses are oriented by walking through the elder room before the staff lounge. The elders are introduced by relationship, not job title. The orientation does not flatter anyone. It tells new hires that they are entering a body of people who already know who they are. The work that follows is judged inside that body, not outside it.

Where is the real We, and who has the right to name it?

The risk is exploitation. Shared origin, family, and place are powerful because they reach below preference. Do not borrow them to smooth a request that mainly serves you. Do not invent closeness. Do not say family when the relationship is merely convenient.

There is a small mirror test before any unity move. Imagine the listener overhearing you explain the cue to a colleague at lunch. Would they nod, or would they feel used? A grandfather's mark on a net survives the lunch table. A vague brand family does not. If the cue cannot survive being explained, the cue should not be used.

The practical limit is also kindly. People know whether they are part of a We before any speaker arrives to remind them. The role of pre-suasion is to make that knowledge salient at the right time, not to invent membership. When a request meets a real We, the answer that follows belongs to the body, not to the asker.

Use unity only where the bond can survive being named aloud by the people inside it.

examples.title: Lea Names the Street on the Envelope

planSpec.audience: an archivist asking families to loan fragile letters
planSpec.stakes: whether shared origin is brought forward before the trust request
planSpec.requiredBeat: the archivist opens with the street name both families left behind before presenting the loan agreement

examples.scenario: A yellowed envelope with an old neighborhood postmark rests beside Lea’s loan agreement. At 3:30 p.m. in the archive reading room, Lea is the archivist deciding whether the shared street belongs before the loan agreement. The family is about to decide whether fragile letters can leave the apartment. Before she presents the form, Lea names the street both families left behind decades ago. The room changes because the request now begins inside shared origin, not institutional custody.
examples.whatToDo: Name the shared street from the postmark before showing the loan agreement. Let real origin carry the trust request.
examples.whyItMatters: The place cue creates a legitimate We. The family is not handing letters to a stranger first; they are speaking with someone tied to the same lost street.

examples.title: Thomas Opens the County Registry

planSpec.audience: a doctor asking nurses to return to their home county
planSpec.stakes: whether place identity makes the request feel like serving one’s own
planSpec.requiredBeat: the doctor points to the county birth registry where three applicants’ families appear before discussing shifts

examples.scenario: A county registry lies open under a clinic lamp while Thomas points to three family names before sliding over the shift roster. Nurses must decide whether returning home is a staffing sacrifice or service to their own county. The registry does not make night shifts easier. It makes place identity present before the roster becomes the whole conversation.
examples.whatToDo: Show the birth-registry names before the shift roster. Let place identity appear before the hard staffing ask.
examples.whyItMatters: The request is heard through belonging to the county, not through vacancy pressure alone. That is unity, not a staffing pitch.

examples.title: Helena Asks About the Net Mark

planSpec.audience: an adviser mediating siblings on boat investment
planSpec.stakes: whether family unity is active before the capital decision
planSpec.requiredBeat: the adviser has each sibling identify the net-mending mark taught by their grandfather before opening the budget

examples.scenario: A repaired net lies across a dock crate while Helena keeps the budget sheet closed. At 6:45 a.m. on the harbor dock, Helena is the family mediator deciding whether the repaired net should be named before the engine budget. “Who made this mark?” she asks. “Granddad,” one sibling says. “He showed all of us,” says another. They must decide whether to fund the boat engine, but Amelia has them identify the net repair mark before any number appears. The budget now enters a room where family unity is active.
examples.whatToDo: Ask each sibling to identify the shared net-mending mark before opening the budget sheet. Bring family identity forward first.
examples.whyItMatters: The investment becomes a decision by people who share a working inheritance. That does not settle the budget, but it changes the ground for cooperation.

examples.title: Ruth Plays the Child’s Clan Greeting

planSpec.audience: a developer asking elders to record pronunciations
planSpec.stakes: whether shared identity precedes technology concerns
planSpec.requiredBeat: the developer plays a child saying the clan greeting before showing the recording consent form

examples.scenario: A small recorder sits beside a handwritten greeting card as Ruth prepares the consent form. The elders are about to decide whether the language app feels useful or extractive. Before the form appears, she plays a child saying the clan greeting. Ruth must decide whether shared identity should be present before technology concerns take the first seat.
examples.whatToDo: Play the child’s clan greeting before showing the consent form. Then explain the recording terms plainly.
examples.whyItMatters: The greeting belongs to the elders’ We before it belongs to the app. It makes the request about continuity, not just technology.

examples.title: David Shows the Doorway Under Water

planSpec.audience: a college officer asking graduates to support flood repairs
planSpec.stakes: whether campus place cues create We before the donation page
planSpec.requiredBeat: the officer shows the flooded doorway everyone used as freshmen before the gift field

examples.scenario: A photo shows a stone campus doorway under floodwater beside David’s gift field and freshman directory. Before the photo, graduates treated the repair appeal like another annual fund email. After he shows the doorway everyone used as freshmen, the gift field changes. The ask still costs money, but the place cue creates a We around a shared threshold.
examples.whatToDo: Show the flooded freshman doorway before the gift field. Let the campus place cue create legitimate shared concern.
examples.whyItMatters: The doorway is common memory, not generic alumni pride. It makes the repair about a place that once held all of them.

examples.title: Eva Starts With the Arrival Pins

planSpec.audience: a coordinator asking attendees to share sensitive documents
planSpec.stakes: whether a shared journey cue makes trust legitimate before intake
planSpec.requiredBeat: the coordinator starts with a map pin exercise of first arrival cities before the document checklist

examples.scenario: A paper map dotted with colored pins rests beside Eva’s document checklist at the immigrant legal-aid intake. Before intake begins, attendees mark first arrival cities and see how many routes led to the same room. Eva knows sensitive documents are next. The map pin exercise does not erase risk, but it makes shared journey visible before people decide what to place on the table. The pin exercise takes ninety seconds and changes which conversation the room has agreed to start.
examples.whatToDo: Begin with the arrival-city map pins before distributing the document checklist. Name the shared journey carefully and briefly.
examples.whyItMatters: The cue builds legitimate trust because the group can see a real pattern of arrival. It must support intake, not exploit vulnerability.

questions.prompt: An archivist names a street both families left behind before asking to borrow fragile letters. Which principle is active?
choices: Unity, because a real shared origin is made conscious before the trust request.
Liking, because the archivist sounds warm.
Scarcity, because the letters are fragile.
questions.explanation: The street creates a We relationship based on shared place. Warmth and fragility may matter, but they are not the central mechanism.

questions.prompt: A rural doctor shows applicants a county birth registry with their family names before discussing shifts. What makes this different from a staffing pitch?
choices: The roster becomes easier to schedule.
The registry makes place identity present before the roster appears.
The doctor avoids mentioning difficult shifts.
questions.explanation: The place cue frames the ask as service to one’s own county. It does not remove hard shifts or solve logistics.

questions.prompt: Siblings argue about boat investment. An adviser asks them to identify their grandfather’s net-mending mark before opening the budget. Why?
choices: The mark proves the engine is affordable.
The mark distracts them from conflict.
The mark makes family unity active before the capital decision.
questions.explanation: The mark brings shared inheritance to consciousness. It does not answer affordability, and distraction would avoid the decision rather than prepare it.

questions.prompt: A developer plays a child saying a clan greeting before asking elders to record pronunciations. What keeps this from becoming exploitation?
choices: The recording device is small and unobtrusive.
The greeting is a legitimate shared identity cue, and consent terms are explained plainly afterward.
The elders are praised before the form appears.
questions.explanation: Unity is clean when the identity cue is real and the request remains transparent. Device size and praise do not protect consent.

questions.prompt: An alumni appeal shows a flooded doorway everyone used as freshmen before the gift field. What does the doorway do? Before the alumni appeal is sent, the fundraiser must decide whether the flooded doorway names a real shared place or exploits nostalgia.
choices: It proves graduates can afford the donation.
It replaces the need for repair details.
It creates a campus We around a shared place.
questions.explanation: The doorway raises shared place identity. It does not establish ability to give, and repair details still have to be clear.

questions.prompt: A legal workshop begins with arrival-city map pins before asking for documents. What is the main caution? At the legal workshop sign-in table, the organizer must decide whether arrival-city pins help people feel seen or expose them.
choices: The pins should be hidden so people do not compare journeys.
The map must support real trust, not mine vulnerability for compliance.
The document checklist should be skipped.
questions.explanation: Shared journey can create unity, but sensitive intake requires care. Hiding the map or skipping documents misses the ethical issue.

questions.prompt: A manager calls employees “family” before asking for unpaid weekend work, though the workplace has high turnover. What is wrong?
choices: The word family is too emotional for any request.
Unity works only with relatives.
The We language is false and borrows intimacy the relationship has not earned.
questions.explanation: False We language exploits unity. Family cues can be legitimate in some contexts, but not when used to cover a one-sided demand.

questions.prompt: A volunteer organizer wants cooperation from neighbors after a flood. Which opening best uses place-based unity? After the flood briefing, the organizer must choose a place cue that invites neighbors into shared repair rather than borrowed intimacy.
choices: Show a map of the shared block and the houses that took water before assigning tasks.
Say everyone should be friendly and positive.
Offer a prize to the first household that signs up.
questions.explanation: The shared block is a legitimate place cue. Friendliness is not unity, and prizes use a different principle.

questions.prompt: How do you tell unity from liking? In a team debrief, the lead must decide whether the cue says we are one group or merely asks people to like the speaker.
choices: Liking depends on warmth toward a person; unity depends on a shared identity experienced as We.
Unity is just liking with stronger emotion.
Liking is ethical and unity is not.
questions.explanation: The distinction is shared identity. Unity may include liking, but it goes deeper than warmth and is not automatically unethical.

reviewCards.front: You are about to choose a unity cue for a community appeal. Which kind of relationship are you reaching for, and how does it differ from liking?
reviewCards.back: A We relationship built on shared identity, family, or place, made visible before cooperation is requested. Unity is deeper than liking: it points to a bond the listener already belongs to, not to a feeling about the speaker.

reviewCards.front: Why is a shared street postmark stronger than a friendly archivist?
reviewCards.back: The postmark names a legitimate shared origin. Friendliness may help, but unity comes from being part of the same We.

reviewCards.front: When does We language become false?
reviewCards.back: When it borrows intimacy or identity that the relationship cannot honestly support, especially to smooth a one-sided request.

reviewCards.front: What does the flooded doorway do in an alumni appeal?
reviewCards.back: It brings shared campus place into awareness before the donation field, making repair feel like care for a place that held them.

reviewCards.front: You are drafting a unity cue for a fundraising letter and want to test whether the bond is real. Which question should you ask before the cue goes into the appeal?
reviewCards.back: Ask who has the right to name this We, and whether the people inside it would recognize the bond as real. If the listener would feel borrowed-from at lunch, the cue should not ship.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is naming a real We before asking for cooperation. You use family, origin, or place cues only when the shared identity is legitimate and the request serves that shared body.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a loan request depends on trust, then name a real shared origin before presenting the agreement.
If you ask people to serve a place, then show the legitimate place connection before the roster or schedule.
If siblings face a capital decision, then surface the shared family marker before the budget.
If shared journey can build trust, then use it briefly and keep consent terms plain.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before one cooperation request, write the exact We you might name. If the people involved would not say it themselves, do not use it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, listen for We language in requests. Mark each one real, stretched, or false, then rewrite one stretched version into a more honest cue.

memorableLines.text: It names a bond that already exists, not one being negotiated in the moment.
memorableLines.why: It names what unity actually is, instead of leaving We as a slogan.

memorableLines.text: Unity can make a request feel like care for a shared body.
memorableLines.why: It captures unity's distinctive effect in a quotable image.

memorableLines.text: Use unity only where the bond can survive being named aloud by the people inside it.
memorableLines.why: It gives the chapter’s standard for legitimate shared identity.

chapters.title: Unity 2: Acting Together
chapters.hook: The rule ballot lands differently after eight oars rise on the same count.
chapters.counterintuition: Shared activity is not unity unless the action creates real togetherness tied to the later ask. Icebreakers pass time; synchronized or collaborative work changes the relationship.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before a cooperation request, design one thirty-second action people can do together that mirrors the support you need from them.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Acting together can create a We before the ask when the shared action directly relates to the cooperation being requested.

breakdown.fastRead:
Oars rise at the same count before dawn practice. Mixed crews row one short cadence together, then the coach opens the launch-rule ballot. The vote is no longer only about restrictions. It follows a shared motion that made safety feel collective.

Unity can come from doing, not only from who people are. People can feel joined by doing one small task before they are asked to help. The act must fit, or it becomes noise pretending to be glue. A random icebreaker is noise. A small shared task tied to the ask gives the request a We to land inside.
breakdown.deepRead:
Two signatures sit on a machine-check tag, one from day shift and one from night shift. The supervisor pairs rivals to inspect the same press before showing the overtime sheet. By the time the request appears, they have already produced one shared fact.

Together is a verb. People discover the body they share when they have just done one small thing inside it.

Source support says We relationships can result from acting together synchronously or collaboratively. Unitary activity arranged before the request can increase liking and support. The illustrations include strangers, teammates, children, students, and consumer-brand relationships, but the narrow point is enough: action can make We before words ask for it.

A therapist uses one pinwheel with anxious children before pair practice. A professor cleans one microscope station alongside students before assigning the rotation. The shared action is small, but it is pointed at the cooperation to come.

The move scales down without losing force. Two strangers folding the same flyer before a city council meeting will speak from a slightly different chair than two strangers walking in cold. The folded flyer is a small object. The shared minute of folding is the larger thing.
breakdown.fullRead:
A table covered with torn package tabs is not a feedback survey yet. Staff and angry customers stand on both sides. The facilitator has them sort failed tabs into trays before the tablet opens. For three minutes, everyone is handling the same broken thing. The survey that follows no longer begins with company versus customer. It begins after a small piece of joint repair.

Hands moving over the same torn tabs make unity by acting together. The action does not have to be grand. It has to be shared, visible, and related to the request. Row before the safety vote. Inspect before the overtime ask. Breathe before pair practice. Clean before the equipment rotation. Sort before the redesign survey. Paint before the mural permit. Arrange chairs before the volunteer signup. Pack supplies before the donor ask.

A neighborhood literacy program does it with chairs. Parents arriving for the first night are asked to help arrange thirty folding chairs into a half-circle before any presentation begins. The chairs were already there. The arrangement is the request, performed in advance. By the time the volunteer signup sheet appears, the parents have already chosen what kind of room this is going to be. The signups follow the seating, not the speech.

A team installing a new patient-handoff protocol in the ICU made the same move. Doctors and night nurses had been arguing for months about who owned the morning report. They spent fifteen minutes filling out a single page together. The page held the previous shift's three unresolved questions. The protocol meeting that followed did not start at zero. It started after the team had already produced one shared answer.

What action would make the request feel like our next step rather than your demand?

A teacher running a parent-school night placed twelve students' essays on a long table, anonymized, and asked parents to pick three they liked. Half the parents read each other's writing for the first time. The reading itself was the lesson the night was supposed to teach. The discussion about curriculum that followed was the cooperation the school had wanted to ask for.

A conference room game can make people laugh and still have nothing to do with the cooperation you need. A forced chant can create synchrony and still feel like theater. The shared action earns its place when it rehearses the support being requested.

Make the act small enough to do in two minutes and specific enough to feel like the next step. The river-cleanup crew that asks volunteers to pick up one piece of glass before introductions has rehearsed the work. The fundraising dinner that asks every table to write one number on a shared napkin has rehearsed the gift. The action does not have to be solemn. It has to be related. The wrong action makes people perform togetherness. The right action lets them notice they were already capable of it.

Act first in miniature. Ask second.

examples.title: Henry Rows Before the Safety Vote

planSpec.audience: a coach asking members to adopt stricter launch rules
planSpec.stakes: whether synchronized warmups make support easier before the vote
planSpec.requiredBeat: the coach has mixed crews row a short cadence together before opening the rule vote

examples.scenario: Oars rise at the same count before dawn practice while Henry holds the rule ballot on the dock. The club is about to decide whether stricter launch rules are worth the hassle. Before opening the vote, he mixes crews and has them row a short cadence together. The stroke count is still in their bodies when the ballots come out.
examples.whatToDo: Have mixed crews row one short cadence together before the rule ballot. Let synchronized safety come before the vote.
examples.whyItMatters: The warmup creates a practical We tied to launch behavior. The rule feels less like control and more like protecting a shared rhythm.

examples.title: Linda Gets Two Shifts on One Tag

planSpec.audience: a supervisor building cooperation between rival shifts
planSpec.stakes: whether collaborative inspection creates We before the overtime request
planSpec.requiredBeat: the supervisor pairs one day worker and one night worker to sign the same machine check before asking for shared overtime

examples.scenario: Two signatures are missing from a machine-check tag when Linda brings the overtime sheet to the press. At 2:05 p.m. beside press three, Linda is the supervisor deciding whether a joint inspection should come before the overtime ask. “Day shift says night leaves the guards loose,” one worker mutters. Linda pairs him with a night worker and says, “Sign this check together first.” They must decide whether overtime is another rival-shift burden or a shared repair after both names are on the same tag.
examples.whatToDo: Pair one day worker and one night worker to complete and sign the same machine check before showing the overtime sheet.
examples.whyItMatters: Collaborative inspection creates a small We around the machine. The overtime request follows shared evidence instead of rivalry.

examples.title: Kate Lets the Pinwheels Spin Together

planSpec.audience: a therapist helping anxious children support one another
planSpec.stakes: whether synchronized breathing changes how they respond to a group task
planSpec.requiredBeat: the therapist has children breathe with the same pinwheel before asking them to practice in pairs

examples.scenario: Pinwheels spin together on a low table while Kate kneels beside the pair cards. The children must decide whether practicing with another child feels scary or manageable. Before pairing them, she has everyone breathe into the same pinwheel rhythm. The room quiets into one pace, and the pair cards no longer feel like being singled out.
examples.whatToDo: Use the shared pinwheel breath before pair practice. Let synchronized breathing create togetherness first.
examples.whyItMatters: The children experience the same rhythm before the task. Pairing follows a shared body cue, not a cold instruction.

examples.title: Lucia Cleans One Microscope With the Group

planSpec.audience: a professor asking students to maintain shared equipment
planSpec.stakes: whether doing the first cleanup together precedes rule acceptance
planSpec.requiredBeat: the professor cleans one microscope station alongside students before assigning the rotation

examples.scenario: A microscope lens cloth lies beside a sign-up strip while Lucia stands at station four. Before the change, students treated the cleanup rotation as punishment. Afterward, she cleans one microscope alongside them before assigning names. The rotation strip appears only after everyone has wiped a lens, checked a slide tray, and seen the equipment as something they maintain together.
examples.whatToDo: Clean one microscope station with the students before assigning the rotation. Make the first act shared.
examples.whyItMatters: The rule follows joint care for the equipment. Students are less likely to hear it as discipline when they have already done the work together.

examples.title: Connor Sorts Failed Tabs With Customers

planSpec.audience: a company asking angry customers to help redesign packaging
planSpec.stakes: whether collaborative action changes the relationship before feedback
planSpec.requiredBeat: the facilitator has customers sort failed package tabs with staff before the survey opens

examples.scenario: A table is covered with torn package tabs while Connor sets a sorting tray beside a survey tablet. Angry customers are about to decide whether feedback will matter. Before the survey opens, he has customers and staff sort the failed tabs by tear point. The tablet waits. For once, both sides are handling the same broken evidence before opinions are collected.
examples.whatToDo: Sort failed tabs with customers and staff before opening the survey tablet. Let repair work precede feedback.
examples.whyItMatters: The relationship changes when both sides handle the same problem. The survey follows collaboration instead of complaint intake.

examples.title: Gina Paints the Test Tile With Owners

planSpec.audience: an organizer asking business owners to back a public art plan
planSpec.stakes: whether shared painting creates support before a permit signature
planSpec.requiredBeat: the organizer has owners paint one test tile together before handing over the permit letter

examples.scenario: A wet ceramic tile sits on a newspaper-covered table while Gina keeps the permit letter in her folder. Business owners each add one brushstroke to the test tile before anyone signs. She watches them lean over the same color edge and talk about the wall as if it is already partly theirs. Only then does the permit letter come out.
examples.whatToDo: Have owners paint one test tile together before handing over the permit letter. Make the first support visible in paint.
examples.whyItMatters: The shared action turns the mural from someone’s proposal into a small joint act. The signature follows participation.

questions.prompt: A rowing coach has mixed crews row one short cadence before a safety-rule vote. Why can that help? At the boathouse before the ballot, the coach must decide whether one shared cadence makes the rule feel like joint safety.
choices: The rowers become too tired to argue.
The rule becomes less strict after rowing.
The synchronized action creates a We tied to launch safety before the ballot.
questions.explanation: The cadence creates togetherness around the same action the rule protects. Fatigue and rule softness are not the mechanism.

questions.prompt: Rival shifts inspect the same machine and sign one tag before an overtime request. Which principle is at work? Beside the press before overtime is discussed, the supervisor must decide why a shared inspection changes the request.
choices: Scarcity, because overtime slots are limited.
Unity through collaborative action before the ask.
Authority, because the supervisor controls the sheet.
questions.explanation: The shared inspection creates We before the overtime ask. Scarcity and authority may be present, but the active move is acting together.

questions.prompt: A therapist has anxious children breathe with the same pinwheel before pair practice. What makes this better than a random icebreaker?
choices: The action directly rehearses calm shared rhythm for the task ahead.
The pinwheel is colorful enough to distract them.
The children cannot refuse after doing it.
questions.explanation: The breathing action relates to the support needed in pair practice. Color and pressure would miss the unity mechanism.

questions.prompt: A professor cleans one microscope with students before assigning cleanup rotation. What changes? In the lab after class, the professor must decide whether cleaning one station together changes the cleanup assignment.
choices: The professor proves students were lazy before.
The equipment no longer needs maintenance.
The rotation becomes a shared-care follow-up, not a cold rule.
questions.explanation: The shared first cleanup creates practical togetherness around the equipment. Blame and elimination of maintenance are not the point.

questions.prompt: A company has angry customers sort broken package tabs with staff before a redesign survey. Why does sequence matter? At the redesign table, the manager must decide why sorting broken tabs together should come before the survey.
choices: The survey follows collaboration with the same evidence.
Customers forget they are angry after handling objects.
Staff gain control over the answers.
questions.explanation: Sorting creates a joint repair frame before feedback. The goal is not forgetting anger or controlling answers; it is changing the relationship honestly.

questions.prompt: Business owners paint one test tile before signing a mural permit letter. What should be avoided? Outside the storefront wall, the owners must decide whether painting one test tile together fits the permit ask.
choices: Letting them see the color before signing.
Using the shared tile as a substitute for explaining permit terms.
Asking more than one owner to participate.
questions.explanation: Shared action prepares support, but it cannot replace clear terms. Seeing color and multiple participants are part of the legitimate action.

questions.prompt: A team leader runs a silly chant before asking for weekend coverage. The chant has nothing to do with the work. What is the weakness?
choices: The shared action is unrelated to the requested cooperation.
Synchrony never affects support.
Weekend requests must always use authority.
questions.explanation: Unitary activity needs fit. A chant may create motion together, but if it does not mirror the needed support, it feels like theater.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood group wants owners to support alley cleanup. Which action best creates unity before the ask? In the alley before the vote, the group must choose a shared action that makes cleanup feel like our next step.
choices: Start with a speech about community spirit.
Offer a discount to the first signer.
Have everyone pick up one visible hazard together, then discuss the cleanup schedule.
questions.explanation: Doing one piece of cleanup together creates a We tied to the ask. Speeches name unity without making it, and discounts use a different road.

questions.prompt: What is the best test for a pre-ask shared action? Before adding any group activity, the planner must decide whether the action mirrors the support being requested.
choices: Does it make people laugh?
Does it create a shared act that resembles the cooperation being requested?
Does it take at least ten minutes?
questions.explanation: Fit to the later cooperation is the test. Humor or duration can help or hurt, but neither defines acting-together unity.

reviewCards.front: How can unity be created without naming shared identity?
reviewCards.back: Through synchronized or collaborative action before the request, especially when the action mirrors the support needed next.

reviewCards.front: Why row before the safety vote?
reviewCards.back: The shared cadence creates a practical We around launch behavior, so the rule follows collective motion rather than a lecture.

reviewCards.front: What makes an icebreaker fail as unity?
reviewCards.back: It is unrelated to the cooperation being requested. Togetherness has to carry into the ask, not just fill time.

reviewCards.front: Why sort broken package tabs before surveying customers?
reviewCards.back: The sorting makes staff and customers handle the same problem together before feedback, changing the relationship from opposition to repair.

reviewCards.front: What is the core sequence for acting-together unity?
reviewCards.back: Do a small related action together first. Make the request second.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is designing a small shared action before the request. The action should rehearse or embody the cooperation you are about to ask for.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you need support for a shared rule, then have people perform the related safe action together first.
If rival groups must cooperate, then pair them on one shared inspection before asking for shared time.
If people resist a care rotation, then do the first care task alongside them before assigning turns.
If you need angry customers to help redesign, then sort the broken evidence with them before opening the survey.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before one cooperation request, design a thirty-second shared action that mirrors the support you need. Do the action first and ask second.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, replace one speech about teamwork with one small act of teamwork. Record whether the request that followed felt different.

memorableLines.text: People discover the body they share when they have just done one small thing inside it.
memorableLines.why: It names what shared action actually does, instead of leaving it as a slogan.

memorableLines.text: The right action lets them notice they were already capable of it.
memorableLines.why: It captures the working theory behind acting before asking.

memorableLines.text: The act must fit, or it becomes noise pretending to be glue.
memorableLines.why: It distinguishes useful unitary activity from icebreaker filler in one sentence.

chapters.title: Ethical Use: A Pre-Pre-Suasive Consideration
chapters.hook: The revenue line looks clean until someone writes the trust cost beside it.
chapters.counterintuition: Ethics is not a polish pass after the tactic works. The first decision is whether the attention plan deserves to exist at all.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before improving one persuasive cue, write three lines: who benefits, who could be misled, and what trust cost would make the cue unacceptable.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Ethical use begins before tactic design: decide whether the pre-suasive setup should be used before deciding how to make it stronger.

breakdown.fastRead:
A pricing mockup sits beside a revenue forecast. The hidden cancellation link adds money to the model. The growth lead circles that line, then writes likely trust cost beside it before approving copy. The tactic has not been built yet, and that is the point.

The ethical decision comes first. Pre-suasion can prepare attention, but it can also exploit it. Commercial pressure often pushes profit ahead of ethics. The answer is not a late disclaimer. It is a pre-pre-suasive test: should this setup be used at all?
breakdown.deepRead:
A campaign manager reads a refill reminder aloud while the patient opt-out list is visible. The message could inform a patient about medicine timing, or it could press anxiety so hard that people feel trapped. She has to decide before sending which side the cue serves.

Working first is not enough. A method that wins attention can still owe people more than it returned.

Source support makes the ethics point directly: pre-suaders face an earlier decision than what to present before a message. They must decide whether using the approach is ethical. The support also warns that profit can outrank ethics and that unethical tactics undermine organizational outcomes in potent ways, though the sidecar does not name those ways.

That is enough to set the rule. If a tactic wins attention by hiding cost, bypassing agency, or exploiting fear, it carries organizational risk as well as moral risk. Trust is not a soft concern when the method depends on receptivity.

There is a quieter cost worth naming. Trust that is spent once on a clever opener is harder to spend the second time. Tactics that succeed today by hiding cost teach the next pitch that hiding is what works. The team learns the wrong lesson alongside the audience.
breakdown.fullRead:
A tablet screen freezes on a sparkling countdown in a children’s game. The price label is visible, but the child presses buy before reading it. In the postmortem, the designer removes the countdown sparkle and strengthens the parent gate. The animation succeeded at attention. It failed the question that should have come before success.
