Ethics has to be upstream because pre-suasion is upstream. Once the cue is polished, the team is already attached to it. Once the metric rises, profit has a lawyer in the room. The pre-pre-suasive move is to stop before craft and ask whether the setup informs, pressures, hides, or confuses.

A nonprofit's grant team learned this with donor pages. Their new design opened with a long tribute photo of one beneficiary, then asked for a credit card before the impact paragraph. Conversion rates rose, then plateaued, then fell. A visitor survey explained why: people who donated quickly reported a slight regret the next week. They were not angry. They were not coming back. The page had moved attention so well that gratitude had not had time to arrive.

A disaster appeal can honor people pictured by checking consent notes and naming specific need. It can also turn suffering into a lever. A wellness form can help employees name goals, or it can prefill goals so agreement looks effortless. An auto-loan script can frame warranty choices clearly, or it can hide total payment until confusion does the work.

A university advising service ran the same audit on its student-retention nudges. The original copy emphasized the cost of dropping out. Retention numbers were fine. Surveys showed students who responded felt scared rather than supported. The team rewrote the nudges to start with the student's own goal sentence from intake. Retention held steady, and the follow-up surveys reported relief instead of pressure. The same outcome, with a cleaner room around it.

Would the person still trust you if they saw the planning note behind the cue?

Do not reduce this to legal compliance. A tactic can meet the minimum and still poison the relationship. The source support’s business warning matters here: unethical pre-suasion damages organizational outcomes. You do not need the unnamed studies to understand the mechanism. People who feel steered become harder to reach next time.

A small habit catches most of these errors. Before any setup ships, the team writes a single paragraph called the planning note. The note covers who the cue points at, what it asks them to do, and what the team did not want to say out loud. If the planning note would embarrass anyone in the room, the cue does not ship. The exercise takes ten minutes. It is cheaper than the trust it protects, and it teaches the team to recognize the same shape in someone else's pitch.

A clean cue can survive daylight. If it cannot, do not optimize it.

examples.title: Paige Writes the Trust Cost Beside Revenue

planSpec.audience: a growth lead deciding whether to hide cancellation terms
planSpec.stakes: whether profit pressure is checked before the attention tactic is built
planSpec.requiredBeat: the lead circles the hidden-fee revenue line, then writes the likely trust cost beside it before approving copy

examples.scenario: A pricing mockup sits beside a revenue forecast while Paige studies a cancellation link buried under account settings. At 10:00 a.m. in the growth review room, Paige is the product lead deciding whether the cancellation mockup passes the ethics check before revenue math. The hidden-fee revenue line looks strong. Before approving copy, she circles the line and writes likely trust cost beside it. She must decide whether the attention tactic should exist before the team improves the page that would hide cancellation terms.
examples.whatToDo: Write the trust cost beside the revenue line before approving copy. Decide whether the hidden-link tactic deserves to exist.
examples.whyItMatters: Profit pressure can corrupt pre-suasion before design begins. Naming trust cost makes ethics part of the first decision, not cleanup.

examples.title: Danielle Reads the Refill Message Aloud

planSpec.audience: a marketing manager weighing fear-based refill messages
planSpec.stakes: whether a health cue informs or exploits patient anxiety
planSpec.requiredBeat: the manager reads the message aloud beside the patient opt-out list before sending it

examples.scenario: A campaign screen shows the opt-out count while Danielle reads the refill message aloud. The line about missing a dose feels sharp enough to move people. It may also exploit anxiety. Before sending, she must decide whether the health cue informs patients or pressures them. The opt-out list stays visible so the cost of fear is in the room.
examples.whatToDo: Read the refill message aloud with the opt-out list visible. Rewrite any line that uses fear beyond what patients need to know.
examples.whyItMatters: A health cue can help or exploit. The opt-out list reminds the team that anxious attention has a relationship cost.

examples.title: Ian Removes the Sparkling Countdown

planSpec.audience: a designer reviewing pre-purchase animations
planSpec.stakes: whether the cue targets the parent’s decision or bypasses the child’s restraint
planSpec.requiredBeat: the designer removes the countdown sparkle after watching a child press buy before reading the price

examples.scenario: A tablet screen is frozen on a sparkling countdown while Ian reviews a session replay. The price label is technically present, and the parent gate appears after one more tap. In the postmortem, he watches a child press buy before reading the price. He removes the countdown sparkle and moves the parent gate forward because the cue bypassed restraint instead of informing a decision.
examples.whatToDo: Remove the countdown sparkle and put the parent gate before the purchase animation. Do not aim the cue at the child’s impulse.
examples.whyItMatters: The animation won attention from the wrong person at the wrong moment. Ethical use requires informed choice, not bypassed restraint.

examples.title: Miriam Rejects the Shocking Photo

planSpec.audience: a fundraising director choosing images for relief donations
planSpec.stakes: whether attention honors the people pictured or turns suffering into a lever
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director rejects the most shocking image after checking consent notes and need specificity

examples.scenario: A contact sheet lies beside a consent log while Miriam holds the need statement for flood repairs. The most shocking image would stop donors cold, but the consent note is unclear and the need it suggests is vague. She rejects it before testing headlines. The appeal will use a less dramatic photo with clear consent and a specific repair need.
examples.whatToDo: Check consent and need specificity before choosing the image. Reject the photo if shock outruns permission or clarity.
examples.whyItMatters: Attention should honor the people pictured. Suffering becomes exploitation when it is used as a lever without consent or a precise need.

examples.title: Vivian Watches the Goal Get Erased

planSpec.audience: an HR manager deciding whether to prefill employee goals
planSpec.stakes: whether the design supports agency or manufactures agreement
planSpec.requiredBeat: the manager watches a tester erase a prefilled goal and marks the coercion risk before launch

examples.scenario: A wellness form has a prefilled goal highlighted while Vivian watches a tester hover over the erase icon. The launch checklist says completion will rise. The tester deletes the goal and says it felt like the company had already chosen for her. Vivian is about to decide whether the cue supports agency or manufactures agreement, and she marks coercion risk in the test note before launch.
examples.whatToDo: Remove prefilled goals and let employees choose or skip the field. Use prompts that support agency instead of manufacturing agreement.
examples.whyItMatters: A prefilled goal can make compliance look like choice. The erase moment shows the design is steering identity, not helping employees decide.

examples.title: Greg Stops the Warranty Script

planSpec.audience: a finance director auditing add-on warranty prompts
planSpec.stakes: whether the pre-suasive frame creates informed choice or confusion
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director has a clerk explain the warranty with the total payment visible and stops the script when the cost is hidden

examples.scenario: A payment worksheet with add-on rows exposed lies between Greg and a finance clerk. At 1:25 p.m. in the dealership finance office, Greg is the buyer deciding whether the exposed add-on rows leave him a real choice. “Explain the warranty,” he says. The clerk covers the total payment and starts with peace of mind. Greg stops him. The customer would have to decide without the cost in view. He has the clerk restart with the warranty row and total payment visible before any comfort language appears.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the warranty row and total payment visible while explaining the add-on. Stop any script that hides cost before comfort language.
examples.whyItMatters: The frame should create informed choice, not confusion. Peace-of-mind language becomes unethical when the price disappears.

questions.prompt: A growth team wants to hide cancellation terms because the revenue forecast improves. What is the pre-pre-suasive move? At the growth review before the experiment ships, the team must decide what standard comes before the profitable cancellation design.
choices: Write the likely trust cost beside the revenue line before approving the tactic.
Improve the copy so fewer people notice the link.
Ask legal whether the link is technically visible.
questions.explanation: The ethical decision belongs before copy optimization. Legal visibility may matter, but trust cost asks whether the tactic should exist at all.

questions.prompt: A refill reminder uses fear to increase medication renewals. What should the manager check first? Before the refill reminder is approved, the manager must decide whether fear serves patient care or just increases renewals.
choices: Whether the message gets the highest click rate.
Whether the cue informs patients or exploits anxiety, with opt-outs visible.
Whether competitors use stronger fear.
questions.explanation: The ethical check asks what the fear cue does to patients and trust. Clicks and competitor behavior can reward exploitation.

questions.prompt: A children’s game uses a sparkling countdown before a price label and parent gate. What is the core problem? In a parent-gate review, the designer must decide whether the countdown pressures children before price is clear.
choices: The animation is too visually polished.
The countdown may bypass a child’s restraint before informed purchase review.
The parent gate should be more colorful.
questions.explanation: The problem is who the cue targets and when. Polish and color are secondary if the design captures child impulse before informed choice.

questions.prompt: A disaster appeal has one shocking image with unclear consent and a vague need. What should the fundraiser do? Before the disaster appeal goes live, the fundraiser must decide whether consent and need are clear enough to use the image.
choices: Use it because attention is scarce during disasters.
Reject it and choose an image with consent and specific need.
Crop out identifying details and keep the shock.
questions.explanation: Consent and need specificity control ethical use. Shock alone can turn suffering into a lever, and cropping may not fix missing permission or vague purpose.

questions.prompt: A wellness form pre-fills employee goals and completion rises. A tester erases the goal and says it felt chosen for her. How should HR read that?
choices: As evidence the design may manufacture agreement rather than support agency.
As proof employees dislike all wellness programs.
As a reason to hide the erase icon.
questions.explanation: The tester’s reaction shows a coercion risk. Hiding the erase icon would deepen the problem, and one test does not condemn every program.

questions.prompt: An auto-loan warranty script starts with peace of mind while the total payment is covered. What makes the frame unethical?
choices: The clerk mentions comfort before mechanics.
The price is hidden while emotional benefit is made salient.
The warranty is optional.
questions.explanation: The frame pushes comfort while removing cost from view, so the choice is not informed. Optional status does not fix hidden payment information.

questions.prompt: A team says a tactic is ethical because it increases profit and passes compliance review. What is the best challenge? At the ethics review table, the team must decide whether profit and compliance are enough when the cue still narrows choice.
choices: Profit is always unethical in persuasion.
Compliance is irrelevant to business outcomes.
Would the tactic damage trust or mislead people if they saw the setup?
questions.explanation: The challenge goes beyond minimum compliance without rejecting profit itself. Ethical pre-suasion asks whether the setup can survive daylight.

questions.prompt: A charity headline focuses donors on urgency, and the funds truly go to the urgent need named. What makes this different from exploitation?
choices: The attention cue is tied to a real need with clear use of funds.
Urgency always makes appeals ethical.
Donors prefer fast decisions.
questions.explanation: Urgency is defensible when it accurately reflects the need and use. Speed alone is not an ethical standard.

questions.prompt: Before improving any pre-suasive cue, which three-line audit is strongest? Before improving the cue, the reviewer must decide what harm, truth, and exit check should come first.
choices: Who benefits, who could be misled, and what trust cost would make the cue unacceptable.
What color, what font, and what button position will lift conversion.
What legal phrase, what approval chain, and what launch date are needed.
questions.explanation: The audit puts ethics before optimization. Design and process details matter later, but they do not answer whether the cue should be used.

reviewCards.front: What is the pre-pre-suasive decision?
reviewCards.back: Whether the attention plan should be used at all, before deciding how to make it more effective.

reviewCards.front: A hidden cancellation link raises revenue. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Write the trust cost beside the revenue gain. Profit does not settle whether the tactic deserves to exist.

reviewCards.front: Why is a child-focused countdown before a purchase risky?
reviewCards.back: It captures the child’s impulse before price and parent review, so the cue bypasses informed choice.

reviewCards.front: What is the daylight test for a persuasive cue?
reviewCards.back: Would the person still trust you if they saw the planning note behind the cue? If not, do not optimize it.

reviewCards.front: Why is ethics not just compliance?
reviewCards.back: A tactic can meet minimum rules and still erode trust, confuse choice, or exploit anxiety in ways that damage future receptivity.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is deciding whether a cue deserves to exist before improving it. You put benefit, possible deception, and trust cost into the plan before conversion pressure takes over.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a design hides cancellation or cost, then write the trust cost beside projected revenue before approving it.
If fear increases response, then read the message beside opt-out data and remove anxiety that does not inform care.
If a cue targets a child before purchase review, then move adult review ahead of the cue.
If comfort language appears before total cost, then stop and make the cost visible first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one cue you planned to improve. Write who benefits, who could be misled, and what trust cost would make it unacceptable before changing a word.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, run a pre-pre-suasive review on a message or screen. Make one decision to remove, soften, or keep a cue based on trust rather than lift.

memorableLines.text: A method that wins attention can still owe people more than it returned.
memorableLines.why: It states the ethics-debt thought in a quotable image.

memorableLines.text: A clean cue can survive daylight.
memorableLines.why: It gives the ethical standard in a memorable line.

memorableLines.text: Ethics has to be upstream because pre-suasion is upstream.
memorableLines.why: It states why ethics must precede tactic design.

chapters.title: Post-Suasion: Aftereffects
chapters.hook: The attic ladder is still down when the insulation quote lands on the calendar.
chapters.counterintuition: A yes created by attention is fragile. Post-suasion starts while the reason is still visible, turning the moment into a next action before it cools.
chapters.tryThisNow: After the next fresh yes, schedule or perform one concrete follow-through while the object, reason, or evidence behind the yes is still in view.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Post-suasion protects the aftereffect by giving a fresh decision an immediate procedure that helps it take root.

breakdown.fastRead:
A pull-down attic ladder hangs under a work light. The auditor holds a thermal photo showing heat loss, and the homeowner has just agreed insulation matters. Before leaving the hatch, the auditor opens the quote calendar. Three days later by email would be too late.

Post-suasion asks what happens after attention has done its work. A temporary shift can fade unless the next action is attached while the reason is still warm. Agreement is not the finish. It is the moment to plant the follow-through.
breakdown.deepRead:
A dietitian places a breakfast swap card beside a glucose meter case. The patient has just decided that morning food is the place to begin. Before checkout, he writes his usual sweet roll on the card and chooses the first swap. The decision gets a procedure before the parking lot steals it.

Fresh yes needs a handle. Without a procedure attached while the reason is still alive, agreement evaporates between the chair and the parking lot.

Source support says pre-suaders want more than temporary changes from momentary shifts in attention. They want those changes to become durable. The support also says two kinds of procedures can increase the chance that initial changes take root, without naming those procedures in the sidecar. That means the safe claim is narrow: design follow-through immediately after the pre-suasive moment.

A donor who verbally pledges can choose exhibit label wording before the pledge card disappears into a folder. A bootcamp student can block Tuesday practice while the solved test is still on screen. Each move gives the new decision somewhere to live.

Procedures do not need to be elaborate. A specific where, when, and what, asked the moment people agree, is usually enough. Where the action happens, when it begins, what the first step looks like. Those three answers, written down within sixty seconds, carry most of the follow-through the moment can earn.
breakdown.fullRead:
The attic photo has power because the homeowner can see heat leaving the house. That power will not last untouched. By Thursday, the inbox will be full, the ladder will be folded, and the draft near the hallway may feel normal again. The quote calendar belongs at the hatch because the reason for action is still present.

This is the aftereffect problem. Pre-suasion can create receptivity, focus, unity, or urgency. Post-suasion asks how the change survives the return to ordinary attention. The safest answer is not a grand habit system. It is a next procedure tied to the moment that produced the yes.

A vaccination clinic does this with appointment cards. The decision to come in for a flu shot is made in the moment when the receptionist asks if September works. The card gets a date written on it before the call ends. Without the date on the card, the agreement is a thought. With the date, it is a small object that will be on the kitchen counter by Tuesday.

At a mailroom recycling reset, residents sort one real item at the station and take a bin guide. At a youth orchestra lesson, the student plays the opening four bars once more and links practice to tuning the stand light. The first repetition matters because the decision is still warm enough to become behavior.

A field-service team running new diagnostics asks technicians, while still in the customer's driveway, to log the day's first surprising fault into the shared sheet. Logging in the driveway is faster, and the entry is more accurate, but the deeper reason is that the technician is briefly in the right mood to do it. By the time the truck reaches the next call, the surprise is already filed.

What is the smallest action that can happen before the reason disappears?

Do not confuse enthusiasm with durability. A donor can feel moved and never send the gift. A patient can agree and forget breakfast by morning. A student can leave proud of a solved bug and never open the editor again. The next action protects the aftereffect from normal life.

Post-suasion does not have to be effortful. A real-estate office that holds a five-minute decluttering walk-through with new clients before they leave the meeting closes more listing contracts than the office that emails a guide. The walk-through is not a separate task. It is the contract starting, and the client knows it. The next action is the proof that the agreement was real.

A library running a new reading-group launch tested both approaches in the same week. One group signed up at a Saturday open house and received an email the following Tuesday with the meeting time. The other group signed up and immediately put a small dot sticker on a calendar by the door. Attendance at the first meeting was thirty percent higher for the sticker group. The work the library cared about had been started at the moment the signup was made.

Hold the door open for the decision while it is still walking through.

examples.title: Emily Opens the Quote Calendar at the Hatch

planSpec.audience: an auditor trying to make a conservation yes last past the visit
planSpec.stakes: whether the next action is locked in while attention is still warm
planSpec.requiredBeat: the auditor schedules the insulation quote before leaving the attic hatch, not three days later by email

examples.scenario: A pull-down attic ladder hangs under a work light while Emily holds a thermal photo beside the quote calendar. The homeowner has just seen heat leaking through the roofline. Claire is about to decide whether to send a quote email later or schedule before leaving the hatch. The reason for saying yes is still glowing in blue and orange on the photo.
examples.whatToDo: Open the quote calendar at the attic hatch and schedule the insulation visit before the ladder folds away.
examples.whyItMatters: The next action attaches while the reason is visible. Waiting for email lets ordinary attention erase the urgency.

examples.title: Mark Writes the First Breakfast Swap

planSpec.audience: a dietitian helping a patient preserve a fresh decision
planSpec.stakes: whether the first durable procedure happens before the patient exits
planSpec.requiredBeat: the dietitian has the patient place one usual breakfast item on a swap card before checkout

examples.scenario: A breakfast swap card sits beside a glucose meter case while Mark reaches for his checkout slip. At 8:50 a.m. in the diabetes clinic checkout line, Mark is the patient deciding how the breakfast swap will survive tomorrow morning. Before the consult, he nodded at general advice and forgot it by the parking lot. Afterward, the dietitian has him write his usual sweet roll on the card and choose tomorrow’s swap before checkout. The decision now has a first breakfast attached to it.
examples.whatToDo: Have the patient write one usual breakfast item and one swap on the card before checkout. Make the first change procedural.
examples.whyItMatters: Agreement becomes more durable when it is tied to tomorrow’s specific meal before the patient leaves the setting that created the yes.

examples.title: Fiona Lets the Donor Choose the Label

planSpec.audience: a development officer making a verbal pledge take root
planSpec.stakes: whether the commitment gets an immediate public or procedural anchor
planSpec.requiredBeat: the officer asks the donor to choose the exhibit label wording before the pledge card goes into a folder

examples.scenario: A draft exhibit label on cream stock rests beside Fiona’s pledge card and label proof. The donor has just said yes to supporting the case. Before the pledge card goes into a folder, Rose must decide whether to simply thank him or ask him to choose the label wording. The commitment can become a future public line while the exhibit is still in his mind.
examples.whatToDo: Ask the donor to choose the exhibit label wording before filing the pledge card. Give the verbal yes an immediate anchor.
examples.whyItMatters: The label choice makes the pledge concrete. The donor leaves with a commitment attached to a visible future artifact.

examples.title: Andrew Blocks Tuesday While the Test Is Green

planSpec.audience: an instructor turning a burst of motivation into weekly practice
planSpec.stakes: whether the next session is placed on the student’s actual calendar
planSpec.requiredBeat: the instructor watches the student block Tuesday’s practice while the solved bug is still on screen

examples.scenario: Andrew watches his student close the fixed-test window beside an open calendar invite. “I finally get it,” the student says. Andrew points to Tuesday. “Put the next practice there before you close the test output.” The student must decide whether the win stays a feeling or becomes a calendar block. Andrew watches the invite land while the green check is still on screen.
examples.whatToDo: Have the student block Tuesday practice before closing the solved test. Tie the next session to the visible win.
examples.whyItMatters: Motivation fades after the screen closes. The calendar invite gives the burst of confidence a place to return.

examples.title: Nina Has Residents Sort One Real Item

planSpec.audience: a building manager making a corrected sorting choice stick
planSpec.stakes: whether the first correct behavior is repeated and marked immediately
planSpec.requiredBeat: the manager has residents sort one real item at the mailroom station and take a printed bin guide

examples.scenario: A mailroom table holds three labeled sample items while Nina stands beside the bin guide. Residents must decide whether the reset is another sign or a corrected habit. Before anyone leaves, each person sorts one real item at the mailroom station and takes the printed guide. The first correct repetition happens in the same place where the old mistake kept happening.
examples.whatToDo: Have residents sort one real item at the station and take the bin guide immediately. Turn the corrected choice into a first repetition.
examples.whyItMatters: The behavior starts before the explanation fades. The guide leaves with a memory of doing the action correctly.

examples.title: Oliver Links Practice to the Stand Light

planSpec.audience: a conductor turning recital excitement into durable practice
planSpec.stakes: whether the child leaves with a named cue and first repetition
planSpec.requiredBeat: the conductor has the student play the opening four bars once more and attach practice to tuning the stand light

examples.scenario: Sheet music rests under a small stand light while Oliver writes a practice card. The student is flushed from recital excitement and ready to promise anything. Oliver has her play the opening four bars once more, then attach tomorrow’s practice to turning on the stand light. The pledge becomes a cue and a first repetition instead of a warm feeling in the hallway.
examples.whatToDo: Have the student play the opening four bars again and write the stand-light cue on the practice card.
examples.whyItMatters: The excitement gets a concrete trigger. Tomorrow’s practice begins with a light switch, not a vague memory of wanting to improve.

questions.prompt: An energy auditor gets a homeowner to agree insulation matters while looking at a thermal photo. What should happen before leaving?
choices: Schedule the quote while the attic hatch and photo are still present.
Send a general follow-up email next week.
Ask the homeowner to think about conservation goals.
questions.explanation: The quote calendar turns the fresh yes into a next action while the reason is visible. Later email and general reflection let the attention shift cool.

questions.prompt: A patient agrees breakfast is the first nutrition target. Which action best protects the decision? At the clinic checkout counter, the nurse must decide what follow-up action protects the breakfast choice after the visit ends.
choices: Give a brochure about healthy eating.
Have the patient write one usual breakfast item and one swap before checkout.
Tell the patient motivation is highest right now.
questions.explanation: The swap card creates an immediate procedure for tomorrow. A brochure and motivation comment do not attach the decision to a specific first behavior.

questions.prompt: A donor verbally pledges to support an exhibit. What makes the pledge more likely to take root? Before the donor leaves the gallery office, the curator must decide how to turn a spoken pledge into a remembered next step.
choices: Thank the donor warmly and end the meeting quickly.
Ask the donor to choose label wording before the pledge card is filed.
Wait a month before discussing public recognition.
questions.explanation: Choosing label wording anchors the pledge in a visible future artifact. Warm thanks are good manners, but they do not create the same follow-through procedure.

questions.prompt: A student fixes a bug and feels motivated to practice. What should the instructor do next?
choices: Praise the student and let the feeling stay pure.
Assign a large weekly plan without checking the calendar.
Watch the student block the next session while the green test is still on screen.
questions.explanation: The calendar block attaches practice to the fresh win. Praise alone fades, and a large plan without a real slot may never happen.

questions.prompt: A building manager explains recycling rules and residents nod. What immediate procedure best creates aftereffect? In the mailroom after the recycling briefing, the manager must decide what residents will practice before the rules fade.
choices: Post a larger sign above the bins.
Have each resident sort one real item at the mailroom station and take a bin guide.
Send a reminder when mistakes happen again.
questions.explanation: The first correct repetition makes the new behavior physical before people leave. Larger signs and later reminders rely on attention returning by itself.

questions.prompt: A conductor wants recital excitement to become practice. Which plan fits post-suasion? At the rehearsal door, the conductor must decide how recital excitement becomes a practice plan before singers go home.
choices: Tell the student to remember how proud she feels.
Ask the parent to buy a nicer music stand.
Have the student play four bars again and attach practice to turning on the stand light.
questions.explanation: The repeat plus stand-light cue converts excitement into a trigger and action. Pride and equipment may help, but they do not create the first procedure.

questions.prompt: A team celebrates agreement on a new safety habit and then adjourns. What is the likely risk? At the safety meeting close, the lead must decide what happens before agreement dissolves into ordinary work.
choices: Celebration always reduces commitment.
Agreement may fade because no immediate follow-through was attached.
The habit must be explained again from the beginning.
questions.explanation: The yes is fragile without a next action. Celebration is not the problem by itself; the missing procedure is.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit gets volunteers excited during orientation. Which next move is strongest? At orientation checkout, the volunteer lead must decide what first action keeps excitement attached to a real shift.
choices: Send a link when staff have time next week.
Tell them enthusiasm proves commitment.
Ask them to schedule their first shift before leaving the room.
questions.explanation: Scheduling the first shift while enthusiasm is present protects the aftereffect. Later links and verbal confidence depend on motivation lasting unaided.

questions.prompt: When is a post-suasive procedure most defensible? Before adding a follow-up device, the planner must decide whether it protects a real choice or merely traps consent.
choices: When it locks people in before they can reconsider.
When it hides how much work the change will take.
When it helps the person enact the choice they just made while the reason is still clear.
questions.explanation: The procedure should support the person’s fresh decision, not trap or mislead them. Durability built on concealment is another ethical problem.

reviewCards.front: You have just received a yes from a tired homeowner at the attic hatch. What is post-suasion actually trying to protect at this moment?
reviewCards.back: The aftereffect of a fresh decision. It turns temporary receptivity into an immediate next action before attention cools.

reviewCards.front: Why schedule the quote at the attic hatch?
reviewCards.back: The thermal photo and open hatch make the reason vivid. Scheduling there attaches action before ordinary attention returns.

reviewCards.front: A patient agrees to change breakfast. What should happen before checkout?
reviewCards.back: Write the usual breakfast item and the first swap on a card. The decision needs a procedure before the setting disappears.

reviewCards.front: A donor verbally pledges and walks out without a next step. What is the risk you have just accepted, and how do you tell?
reviewCards.back: A yes can be temporary. Without an immediate anchor, normal life may erase the attention shift that created it.

reviewCards.front: What makes a post-suasive procedure ethical?
reviewCards.back: It helps the person enact a choice they just made with the reason still clear, rather than locking them in or hiding effort.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is designing the first after-action. Once attention has produced a yes, you attach the next step while the reason for action is still visible.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a homeowner agrees after seeing evidence, then schedule the next visit before the evidence is put away.
If a patient chooses a target behavior, then write the first specific swap before checkout.
If a student feels motivated by a solved problem, then block the next practice session before closing the screen.
If residents accept a corrected rule, then have them perform one correct action at the problem site immediately.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: After one fresh yes today, do not end the conversation until one next action is scheduled, written, or performed while the reason is still visible.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each week, list three agreements you helped create. For each, note the immediate procedure that followed or the gap where the yes was left to cool.

memorableLines.text: Agreement is not the finish. It is the moment to plant the follow-through.
memorableLines.why: It states both the correction and the action it implies.
